concepts.label: Gender Division and the Public/Private Division
concepts.cardText: Gender division is a hierarchical social division. It is seen as natural and unchangeable, but it is based on social expectations and stereotypes, not biology. Boys and girls are brought up to believe women's main responsibility is housework and children, giving a sexual division of labour: women do the work inside the home, men the work outside. When these jobs are paid for, men take them up. Women's work is not valued, and their role in public life, especially politics, is minimal.

concepts.label: Disadvantages Women Face in India
concepts.cardText: India is still a male-dominated, patriarchal society. The literacy rate among women is 54 per cent against 76 per cent among men, and girls drop out because parents prefer to spend on boys' education. Women are few in highly paid jobs; an average woman works one hour more a day than a man, but much of her work is unpaid and not valued. Despite the Equal Remuneration Act, 1976, women are paid less than men. Sex-selective abortion has brought the child sex ratio down to 919, and women face harassment and violence.

concepts.label: Women's Political Representation
concepts.cardText: Feminists concluded that unless women control power, their problems will not get adequate attention, so more women are needed as elected representatives. In India, women reached 14.36 per cent of the Lok Sabha only in 2019, and are under 5 per cent in State Assemblies. One-third of seats in panchayats and municipalities are reserved for women, giving more than 10 lakh elected women representatives. The Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam, 2023 gives 33 per cent reservation in the Lok Sabha, State Assemblies and the Delhi Assembly.

concepts.label: Communalism
concepts.cardText: The problem begins when religion is seen as the basis of the nation and is expressed in politics in exclusive and partisan terms: one religion is presented as superior, demands are made against another group, and state power is used to dominate. Communal politics is based on the idea that religion is the principal basis of social community, so followers of one religion are one community with the same interests. In its extreme form, people of different religions cannot live as equal citizens in one nation. This belief is fundamentally flawed: there are many voices inside every community.

concepts.label: Secular State
concepts.cardText: The makers of our Constitution chose the model of a secular state. There is no official religion for the Indian state, unlike Buddhism in Sri Lanka, Islam in Pakistan and Christianity in England. The Constitution gives everyone freedom to profess, practice and propagate any religion, or none; it prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion; and it allows the state to intervene in religion to ensure equality within religious communities, for example by banning untouchability. A secular Constitution is necessary but not sufficient to combat communalism.

concepts.label: Caste Inequalities
concepts.cardText: Unlike gender and religion, caste division is special to India. In the caste system, hereditary occupational division was sanctioned by rituals; members of a caste practised similar occupations, married within the group and did not eat with other castes. The system was based on exclusion of and discrimination against 'outcaste' groups through untouchability. Reformers like Jotiba Phule, Gandhiji, B.R. Ambedkar and Periyar Ramaswami Naicker worked against it. With economic development, urbanisation, education, occupational mobility and the weakening of landlords, the old notions of caste hierarchy are breaking down.

concepts.label: Caste Has Not Disappeared
concepts.cardText: Caste has not disappeared from contemporary India. Most people still marry within their own caste or tribe, and untouchability has not ended completely. Effects of centuries of advantages and disadvantages continue: groups that had access to education did well in modern education too, so 'upper castes' are disproportionately present in the urban middle classes. Caste is still closely linked to economic status: average economic status follows the old hierarchy, extreme poverty is much higher for the lowest castes, and upper castes are over-represented among the rich.

concepts.cardText: Like communalism, casteism is rooted in the belief that caste is the sole basis of social community, a belief not borne out by experience. concepts.label: Elections Are Not All About Caste
concepts.cardText: Elections are not all about caste. No parliamentary constituency has a clear majority of one caste, so every candidate needs support from more than one caste. No party wins all the votes of a caste; a 'vote bank' only means a large proportion of a caste votes for a party. Many parties may field candidates from the same caste, and ruling parties and sitting MPs and MLAs frequently lose. Party attachment, economic interests and people's assessment of the government's performance also matter.

concepts.label: Politics in Caste
concepts.cardText: Politics also influences caste: it is not politics that gets caste-ridden, it is caste that gets politicised. Caste groups try to become bigger by incorporating neighbouring castes, enter into coalitions and negotiation with other castes, and new groups such as 'backward' and 'forward' castes appear. Caste politics has given disadvantaged communities, such as Dalits and OBCs, better access to decision making. But politics based on caste alone can divert attention from poverty, development and corruption, and can lead to tension, conflict and violence.
